author: Vitor
aiExplanation: This solution first collects every **pairwise XOR** value `nums[j] ^ nums[k]` (including `j === k`) into a `set` using a nested loop, then combines each element of `nums` with every value already stored in that set to build a second `overallSet` of all possible **triplet XOR** results, finally returning its size; the issue is that the inner set can hold close to `n^2` distinct values, so combining it with every element of `nums` again pushes the total work toward `O(n^3)`, which is too slow and causes the **TLE**.

author: Vitor
aiExplanation: This attempt only fills `pairSet` with XOR values from **strictly distinct** index pairs (`k` starts at `j + 1`), skipping the case `j === k`; because a valid triplet allows `i <= j <= k`, this drops triplets where two of the three chosen elements are the same array position, and with a single-element array the inner loop never runs at all, so `pairSet` stays empty and the function incorrectly returns `0`, which is why it **fails**.

author: Vitor
aiExplanation: This version patches the previous bug by special-casing `n === 1` (returning `1` immediately), and otherwise builds `pairSet` from strictly distinct pairs before combining it with each element of `nums` into a `seen` set of triplet XOR results; while now correct, the algorithm still costs `O(n^2)` to build `pairSet` and then up to `O(n * n^2)` to combine it with every element, so the overall `O(n^3)` behavior remains too slow for large inputs and results in a **TLE**.

author: Vitor
aiExplanation: This accepted solution exploits the fact that XOR results are bounded (values up to `1500` fit within `maxi = 2048`), so instead of using `Set` objects it marks reachable XOR values with fixed-size **boolean arrays**: `pairXor` records every achievable pairwise XOR in `O(n^2)`, and then `tripletXor` is filled by combining each *possible* pairwise XOR value (only `maxi` of them, not `n^2`) with every element of `nums`, giving an `O(n^2 + maxi * n)` runtime that comfortably fits within the limits, and the final answer is just the count of `true` entries in `tripletXor`.
